Project calculation

How to read the model

Measured geometry: visible cladding cuts, decking and opening counts come from the supplied conceptual model.

Schematic framing: extra lumber is an assumed counting layout with spacing and section sizes disclosed. It is not structural design, a full cut list or a procurement specification. Blocking, connectors, bracing and deck framing are not individually quantified.

Surface proxy: sheets, insulation, paint and roof coverage use envelope surfaces. The highlighted surface shows location, not separate physical layers or every purchased unit.

Unmeasured scope: MEP routing, detailed foundation quantities and some supporting materials remain package allowances. Selecting them shows that limitation explicitly. Furniture, landscaping and the display ground are excluded.

Cost boundary: rates bundle assumed installation labor and incidental materials; the 15% default markup is an additional contractor charge. Sales tax, freight and subcontractor markups are not separately verified. Quotes must state these inclusions.

Quantity basis, sources and allocation method

Geometry source [Q0]: the existing Plana House conceptual reconstruction from the attached plan, issue 02 dated 06.06.26. Model envelope: 12.25 × 4.15 m, wall height 2.625 m above finished floor, 45° roof and 0.10 m roof overhangs. The architectural geometry is approximate; the new stud, joist, plate, header and rafter layout is an estimating assumption, not extracted from structural drawings. Conversion: 1 ft = 0.3048 m; 1 sq ft = 0.09290304 m².

Roof coverage example [Q1]: McElroy Metal, Max-Rib official product specifications list a 36-inch effective cover width (accessed September 10, 2026). This is the width assumed for the roof LF calculation: each linear foot covers 3 sq ft before end-of-run excess and waste. The model's seam graphic is schematic, not a fabrication layout. This source supports an example coverage width only; it provides none of the unit rates used here.

Price basis [A0]: every initial unit rate is an unsourced allocation of the prior budget, as shown below. Rate = allocated allowance ÷ priced quantity, rounded to $0.01. Extension = priced quantity × rate, rounded to $0.01. Project total = direct + contractor markup + site/utilities + design + permits + contingency on that combined amount. No separate material-versus-labor split, licensed RSMeans rate or supplier quotation has been obtained. Editing a rate replaces that assumption; it does not alter geometry.

Original packageChosen allocation to takeoff linesOriginal base allowance

Scope boundaries: plumbing includes pipework and fixture hookup labor; kitchen and bathroom rows include fixture supply/positioning. Kitchen countertop includes sink/tap supply; appliances are separate. Bathroom tile is deducted from timber flooring. Paint is separate from lining installation. Roof trim is separate from panels. Envelope sheathing is one assumed layer per floor, wall and roof surface. Foundation packages include their connection work; no second concrete or steel material charge is added.

Uncertainty: the earlier $139,315–$342,600 low/high scenarios remain judgmental, not statistical confidence limits. They are retained in the historical audit below, do not reprice with your edits, and are not independently validated by the new quantity takeoff. Contractor and supplier quotations, location, site data, structural design, MEP layouts and selected products are needed to replace the remaining assumptions.

Historical budget & source audit

The earlier $220,000 figure was an illustrative allowance, not an independently validated construction estimate. No local contractor bids, supplier quotations, permit calculation or licensed estimating-database unit prices have been obtained. The amounts below remain provisional.

What this audit changes

The arithmetic is reproducible, but reputable background sources do not prove the assumed prices. This revision replaces the commercial ADU cost-guide reference with a primary builder survey, university research and official fee guidance, identifies the actual age and scope of each source, and labels every unsourced dollar allowance. It does not increase confidence in the $220,000 figure simply by adding citations.

This page supersedes the estimate-basis statements in the earlier PDF and ZIP exports. Those earlier exports have not been revised.

1. Evidence, assumptions and arithmetic

LabelMeaning in this estimate
Published evidenceA fact reported by a named source, with its date and scope. Used for context and scope checks, not as a project-specific quote.
Model quantityA quantity calculated from the existing conceptual model. Approximate geometry is not an engineered material takeoff.
AllowanceA judgmental amount chosen for the original budget. No independent source currently establishes that this amount will buy the specified work locally.
CalculatedA subtotal, percentage or total obtained from the displayed allowances.

All 13 direct construction amounts below are allowances. The contractor percentage, site budget, design budget, permit budget and contingency percentages are also assumptions. None is represented as an RSMeans rate, a builder bid or a government fee calculation.

2. The exact calculation

Direct construction: $10,000 + $25,000 + $9,000 + $11,000 + $12,000 + $10,000 + $11,000 + $7,000 + $6,000 + $9,000 + $6,000 + $9,000 + $6,000 = $131,000

House including contractor charges: $131,000 × 1.15 = $150,650

Before contingency: $150,650 + $20,000 site/utilities + $12,000 design/engineering + $7,000 permits = $189,650

Total: $189,650 × 1.15 = $218,097.50, rounded to a $220,000 working allowance.

The first 15% is assumed contractor overhead and profit, applied to direct house work only. Site/utilities are treated as a separate all-in package, so no second contractor markup is added to them. The second 15% is an assumed contingency on the entire pre-contingency project budget. Neither percentage is prescribed by the sources.

How to read the range: $139,315–$342,600 (approximately $140,000–$345,000) is the result of three sets of chosen inputs. It is not a statistically supported confidence interval or a verified local market range. Actual project costs can fall outside it. Dollar-level precision shows the math, not the accuracy of the inputs.

5. Source register and limits

Sources checked September 10, 2026. Publication or data dates are shown separately; the audit date does not make historical prices current.

S1 · Plana Architecture — project owner / designer

Plana House project page identifies 42 m² of internal area and an adaptable timber dwelling concept. This supports the design description, not a construction price. Existing model metadata identifies the earlier source plans as issue 02, 06.06.26.

S2 · National Association of Home Builders — primary builder survey

Cost of Constructing a Home—2024, January 20, 2025, Table 1 / PDF page 3: $428,215 of construction cost for a sample home averaging 2,647 finished sq ft, or $161.77/sq ft. The study used 41 usable builder responses and cautions against treating it as a location-specific estimating tool.

Its construction total includes some design/permit/site costs, while overhead and profit are separate. Our categories differ. The report's $38,248 overhead plus $72,971 profit equals about 26% of its construction cost; this does not establish our assumed 15% contractor markup. No survey percentage or $/sq-ft figure was mechanically applied to this house.

S3 · UC Berkeley Center for Community Innovation — primary ADU owner research

Implementing the Backyard Revolution, April 2021, Table 2 / PDF page 11, reports separate medians of $180,000 construction cost and $300/sq ft for detached ADUs. The survey was conducted in 2020 and mainly covered 2018–2019 California projects.

Detached units are the closer typology; the $150,000 / $250-sq-ft headline for all ADUs includes other unit types and is not used here as the detached-house benchmark. These are historical, self-reported California costs with sampling limitations. They have not been escalated to 2026, and differences in cost inclusions prevent a direct match to our total.

S4 · Gordian / RSMeans — professional estimating methodology

How Location Impacts Construction Costs, March 12, 2025, explains how labor, materials, climate and local requirements affect pricing. This supports the need for a location-specific estimate. No licensed RSMeans unit-cost database or city-cost factor was accessed or applied.

S5 · Santa Cruz County — official fee-estimating guidance

ADU fee estimator guidance says fees depend on entered project information and that its tool excludes non-County agency fees. This illustrates why a local fee calculation is needed. The tool was not run for this property and does not support the assumed $7,000 fee allowance. Santa Cruz is not the assumed building location.

S6 · Portland — local bedroom-size example only

Portland Code 29.30.210 sets a 70 sq ft sleeping-room minimum with stated exceptions. It supports flagging room size for review, not a finding that this is the applicable code at your site.

Evidence conclusion: These sources are more authoritative, but they do not independently validate any of the 13 project-specific prices. The commercial GreatBuildz reference and the materials-only inflation discussion have been removed from the basis. No inflation multiplier, market-location factor or unsupported accuracy percentage has been added.

6. What would make this a locally credible estimate?

Required project inputs

  • City/state or country, intended start date, and currency.
  • Standalone dwelling or ADU; parcel access, utility distance/capacity and site slope.
  • Soil/foundation approach, local structural and energy requirements, and resolved bedroom layouts.
  • Cladding, roof, windows, kitchen, bathroom and interior finish schedules.

Pricing evidence to replace the allowances

  • Local builder/subcontractor quotes tied to the same drawings, scope and exclusions.
  • Supplier quotes or current localized assembly/unit prices for the specified products.
  • Published local permit schedules and property-specific utility charges.
  • Separate contractor terms and a project-specific contingency assessment. A higher contingency cannot repair missing scope.

Sensitivity, not a prediction: Keeping other base inputs fixed, each additional $10,000 of direct house work adds $13,225 after the assumed contractor markup and contingency. Each additional $10,000 of site/fee/design cost adds $11,500. This shows why local inputs matter.

Included in the provisional scope

  • Timber dwelling, conceptual pier/pad foundation and insulated floor; metal roof and ordinary timber cladding.
  • Four windows, two exterior door assemblies, internal finishes and basic kitchen/bathroom equipment.
  • Plumbing/hot water, electrical work, heating/cooling and ventilation allowances.
  • Small decks, entrance canopy, site/utilities, local design, ordinary permits and separate contingency.

Excluded from the provisional scope

  • Land, financing/carrying costs, property taxes and legal/transaction costs.
  • Demolition, long driveways/utilities, retaining walls, rock excavation or contaminated ground.
  • New well/septic, extraordinary utility/off-site charges, solar/batteries and loose furniture.
  • Premium custom finishes and enlargement needed for local compliance. Requirements for excluded work increase the budget.
Bedroom layout remains an unresolved scope riskBedroom 2 in the existing reconstruction is about 5.1 m² (55 sq ft), with a narrow dimension near 1.8 m. Both bedrooms, escape windows, ceiling heights and circulation require local review. The model preserves the supplied concept; it does not certify two legal bedrooms. Enlarging or substantially redesigning the house is not priced.

Model accuracy

The earlier reconstruction used P.101 for room positions, S.101–S.104 for roof/relative heights and E.101–E.103 for openings. The published internal area is distinct from the exterior footprint. Floor level, support count, wall build-ups, opening details, canopy supports and furniture are interpretations. There are no structural calculations or concealed service layouts.

Using the model

Garden and Entrance show the long elevations. Cutaway and Plan reveal the layout. Drag to orbit and scroll/pinch to zoom. Roof and view controls change only the display. The material takeoff above now adds quantity highlights and editable rates that recalculate its current allowance. The downloadable timber-clad GLB is a conceptual mesh in metres, not engineered BIM or permit documentation.
